title: The slope is covariance over variance
objectives: Derive the least squares slope and intercept.
Compute them from deviations, or from a correlation and two standard deviations.

screens.title: Five days and a ring
screens.prose: Five more days of a market's and a stock's returns, in per cent. The ring marks the average day, $(\bar x, \bar y) = (1, 1)$. Find the least squares line, then see where it runs.
screens.question: Slide both until the sum of squared residuals is as small as you can make it.

hints.text: Tilt the line first, then move the intercept.
Days 1 and 5 sit far from the ring. They decide the tilt.
Try slope 1.3 and intercept $-0.3$.

feedback.correct: The lowest sum is 3.1, at slope 1.3 and intercept $-0.3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the number in the corner stops falling whichever way you move.

byKey.flat: Your line is nearly flat, so days 1 and 5 miss by a lot. Tilt it upwards.
byKey.off: Close, but not the lowest yet. Move one slider at a time and keep each move that lowers the corner.

explain.text: The best line is $\hat y = -0.3 + 1.3x$, with a sum of 3.1. It runs straight through the ring: at $x = 1$ it gives $-0.3 + 1.3 = 1 = \bar y$. The derivation below shows this always happens.

screens.title: Measuring from the average day
screens.prose: Measure every day from the average day. Its **deviations** are $x_i - \bar x$ and $y_i - \bar y$, with $\bar x = 1$ and $\bar y = 1$. A positive deviation means above the average.
screens.question: Fill in the two deviations for each day.

hints.text: Subtract 1 from every $x$ and from every $y$.
Day 1 sits left of and below the ring, so both its deviations are negative.

feedback.correct: Each column of deviations adds to 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each deviation is the value minus 1, the mean, keeping the sign.

explain.text: Each deviation says how far a day sits from the average, and its sign says which side. Both columns add to 0, as deviations from a mean always do. Days 1 and 5 are far out on the same side in both directions.

screens.title: Products and squares
screens.prose: For each day, multiply the two deviations, and square the $x$ deviation. Then add each column. We call the sums $S_{xy} = \sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)$ and $S_{xx} = \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$.
screens.question: Fill in the products, the squares and the two sums.

hints.text: A product of two negatives is positive.
Day 1 gives $(-2)(-3) = 6$, the same as day 5.
Products: 6, 1, 0, 0, 6, summing to 13. Squares: 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, summing to 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply across each row, keeping signs, and square the first deviation.

explain.text: The products add to $S_{xy} = 13$ and the squares to $S_{xx} = 10$. Days 1 and 5 give the big products, because they sit far out on the same side in both. Day 3 has $x$ at its average, so it adds nothing to either sum.

screens.title: Slope, then intercept
screens.prose: Divide the two sums: $S_{xy}/S_{xx} = 13/10 = 1.3$, the slope you found with the sliders. The line also ran through the ring, $(\bar x, \bar y) = (1, 1)$.
screens.question: Using the slope 1.3 and the ring, what is the intercept $a$?

hints.text: The line passes through $(1, 1)$, so $1 = a + 1.3 \times 1$.
Read where the line crosses $x = 0$.
$a = \bar y - b\bar x = 1 - 1.3 \times 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the point $(1, 1)$ into $y = a + 1.3x$ and solve for $a$.

byKey.sign: You worked out $b\bar x - \bar y$. The intercept is $\bar y - b\bar x$, which is negative here.
byKey.mean: $\bar y$ is the height at $x = 1$, not at $x = 0$. Step back one unit along the slope.
byKey.added: You added $b\bar x$ to $\bar y$. Going back from $x = 1$ to $x = 0$ lowers the line by 1.3.

explain.text: The line passes through $(1, 1)$, so $1 = a + 1.3$ and $a = -0.3$. In general $a = \bar y - b\bar x$. The line climbs 1.3 per unit, so at $x = 0$ it sits 1.3 below $\bar y$.

screens.title: Why the sums give the slope
screens.prose: Now the general case. Minimise $S(a, b) = \sum (y_i - a - bx_i)^2$ by setting both partial derivatives to 0. *The normal equations* (Orthogonality and Least Squares) reached the same line by projection.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\partial S/\partial a = -2\sum (y_i - a - bx_i) = 0$, the condition for the intercept
$\bar y - a - b\bar x = 0$, so $a = \bar y - b\bar x$, dividing by $-2n$
$\partial S/\partial b = -2\sum x_i (y_i - a - bx_i) = 0$, the condition for the slope
$\sum x_i \big((y_i - \bar y) - b(x_i - \bar x)\big) = 0$, substituting $a = \bar y - b\bar x$
$\sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) = b\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$, replacing $x_i$ by $x_i - \bar x$, which subtracts $\bar x$ times sums of deviations, both 0

hints.text: Start with the intercept's condition: it gives $a$ in terms of $b$.
The substitution line needs $a = \bar y - b\bar x$ already found.
Intercept condition, solve for $a$, slope condition, substitute, centre the $x_i$, divide.

feedback.correct: Two conditions, one substitution, one division.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $a$ from the first condition before substituting it into the second.

byKey.d3: The slope condition is used after we know $a$ in terms of $b$. Start with the intercept's condition.
byKey.d4: Substituting needs $a = \bar y - b\bar x$ first, from the intercept's condition.
byKey.d5: Centring the $x_i$ comes after the substitution.
byKey.d6: Dividing by $S_{xx}$ is the last step.

explain.text: Line 2 says the best line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$, which is why it ran through the ring. Line 6 is the slope you computed, $13/10$. The projection route gave the same formulas because both minimise the same sum.

screens.title: Covariance over variance
screens.prose: Divide the top and bottom of $S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ by $n - 1$: $$b = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x, y)}{\mathrm{Var}(x)} = r\,\frac{s_y}{s_x}, \qquad a = \bar y - b\bar x.$$ The second form uses $r = \mathrm{Cov}(x, y)/(s_x s_y)$ from *Moving together* (Random Variables).
screens.question: For our five days, what is $\mathrm{Cov}(x, y)$, dividing by $n - 1$?

byKey.by-n: You divided by $n = 5$. With $n - 1 = 4$ it is 3.25; either way the divisor cancels in $b$ if you use it top and bottom.
byKey.sum: 13 is the sum of products. Divide it by $n - 1$.

explain.text: $\mathrm{Cov}(x, y) = 13/4 = 3.25$ and $\mathrm{Var}(x) = 10/4 = 2.5$, so $b = 1.3$ again. The divisor cancels, so it only matters that top and bottom use the same one. Also $r = 13/\sqrt{10 \times 20} = 0.919$ and $0.919 \times \sqrt{20/10} = 1.3$.

screens.title: Spread is not slope
screens.prose: Another stock has correlation $r = 0.4$ with the market. The market's daily standard deviation is 1.2%, and the stock's is 2.4%.
screens.question: What is the slope of the stock's return on the market's?

hints.text: Which form of the slope uses $r$ and the two standard deviations?
$b = r\,s_y/s_x$, with $y$ the stock.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $b = r\,s_y/s_x$, with the stock as $y$.

byKey.no-r: You divided the spreads and left out $r$. That is the slope only when every point lies on the line, $r = 1$.
byKey.swapped: You put $s_x$ over $s_y$. We predict the stock from the market, so the stock's spread goes on top.
byKey.r-only: $r$ is the slope only when both spreads are equal. Here the stock is twice as volatile.

explain.text: $b = 0.4 \times 2.4/1.2 = 0.8$. A stock twice as volatile as the market can still have a slope below 1, because only part of its movement goes with the market. Using $s_y/s_x = 2$ alone assumes a perfect fit.

screens.title: The other regression
screens.prose: A colleague regresses the other way: market on stock, $\hat x = c + dy$. Same five days, same sums, and $S_{yy} = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2 = 20$. Their line is dashed, drawn on our axes.
screens.question: What is their slope $d$?

hints.text: Swap the roles: now $y$ is the predictor.
The deviations of the predictor are squared on the bottom.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $x$ predicted from $y$, divide $S_{xy}$ by $S_{yy}$.

byKey.inverted: You inverted our slope, $1/1.3$. The reverse regression minimises horizontal misses, so it has its own slope, $S_{xy}/S_{yy}$.
byKey.same: Swapping the roles changes the slope. The bottom becomes the sum of squared $y$ deviations.

explain.text: $d = S_{xy}/S_{yy} = 0.65$, not $1/1.3 = 0.77$. On our axes the dashed line climbs $1/0.65 = 1.54$ per unit, steeper than 1.3, though both lines pass through the ring. The two agree only when $r = \pm 1$, since $b \times d = r^2 = 0.845$.

screens.title: When $r$ is 0
screens.prose: Five new points. Their products of deviations cancel exactly: $S_{xy} = 0$, so $r = 0$. The ring is their average day, $(1, 0.6)$.
screens.question: What is the least squares line?

options.text: $\hat y = 0.6$, a flat line at $\bar y$

options.why: $r = 0$ makes the slope 0, not the intercept. The line still passes through $(\bar x, \bar y) = (1, 0.6)$.

options.text: There is no line: with $r = 0$ there is nothing to fit
options.why: There is always a least squares line. With $b = 0$ it is the best flat line.

options.text: $\hat y = -0.1 + 0.7x$, through the ring and the last point
options.why: You joined two points. The products on the left and right cancel, so any tilt raises the sum of squares.

hints.text: What does $b = r\,s_y/s_x$ give when $r = 0$?
The line must still pass through the ring.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $b$ from $r = 0$, then use $a = \bar y - b\bar x$.

byKey.zero: $r = 0$ makes the slope 0, not the intercept. The line still passes through $(1, 0.6)$.
byKey.none: There is always a least squares line. With $b = 0$ it is the best flat line.

explain.text: With $r = 0$ the slope is 0 and $a = \bar y = 0.6$: the best flat line from lesson 1. Yet these points clearly follow a U. $r = 0$ means no straight-line relation, not no relation.

screens.title: Beta from a risk report
screens.prose: A risk report gives a technology stock an annual volatility of 30% and its index 15%. The correlation between their returns is 0.6.
screens.question: What is the stock's beta, the slope of its returns on the index's?

hints.text: Beta is a slope, so $\beta = \rho\,\sigma_s/\sigma_m$.
The stock is the $y$, so its volatility goes on top.

byKey.no-rho: You divided the volatilities and dropped the correlation. That would be beta only if the stock tracked the index perfectly.
byKey.swapped: You put the index volatility on top. We regress the stock on the index, so the stock's goes on top.
byKey.rho: The correlation alone ignores that the stock is twice as volatile as the index.

explain.text: $\beta = \rho\,\sigma_s/\sigma_m = 0.6 \times 30/15 = 1.2$. Annual or daily volatilities give the same beta, as long as both use the same horizon. A beta of 1.2 is typical for a large technology stock.

screens.title: A hedge ratio
screens.prose: A desk holds £5m of a corporate bond and hedges it with gilt futures. The hedge ratio $h$ is the slope from regressing the bond's daily % changes on the future's. Over a year the figures are below.
screens.question: How much of the future should the desk sell, in £?

hints.text: The bond is $y$ and the future is $x$.
The slope divides the covariance by the predictor's variance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $h = \mathrm{Cov}/\mathrm{Var}(\text{future})$, then scale the £5m position.

byKey.wrong-way: You divided by the bond's variance, which regresses the future on the bond. The predictor is the future, so divide by its variance.
byKey.one-for-one: Selling £5m assumes the bond moves one for one with the future. The regression says it moves 0.75 for 1.

explain.text: $h = 0.30/0.40 = 0.75$, so the desk sells £3.75m of futures. Dividing by the bond's variance regresses the wrong way and over-hedges, at £4.17m. The residuals of this regression are the risk the hedge leaves behind.

ideas: Setting both partial derivatives of $S(a, b)$ to 0 gives $a = \bar y - b\bar x$, so the line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$.
The slope is $b = S_{xy}/S_{xx} = \mathrm{Cov}(x, y)/\mathrm{Var}(x) = r\,s_y/s_x$; the projection route in Orthogonality and Least Squares gives the same.
Regressing $x$ on $y$ gives a different line unless $r = \pm 1$. With $r = 0$ the line is flat at $\bar y$.

formula.name: Least squares slope and intercept
formula.tex: b = \dfrac{\mathrm{Cov}(x, y)}{\mathrm{Var}(x)} = r\,\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}, \qquad a = \bar y - b\bar x
formula.note: Beta is $\rho\,\sigma_s/\sigma_m$; a hedge ratio is the same slope for one asset's changes on another's.

summary.trap: The ratio of spreads $s_y/s_x$ is not the slope: it needs the factor $r$, and swapping $x$ and $y$ gives a different line.

quiz.prose: A regression has $\bar x = 0.2$, $\bar y = 0.5$ and slope $b = 1.5$.
quiz.question: What is the intercept $a$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $a = \bar y - b\bar x$.

byKey.added: You added $b\bar x$. The line must drop by $b\bar x$ going back to $x = 0$.
byKey.sign: You computed $b\bar x - \bar y$. Reverse it: $\bar y - b\bar x$.

explain.text: The line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$, so $a = \bar y - b\bar x = 0.5 - 1.5 \times 0.2 = 0.2$.

quiz.prose: For two return series, $\mathrm{Cov}(x, y) = 1.8$, $\mathrm{Var}(x) = 1.5$ and $\mathrm{Var}(y) = 4$.
quiz.question: What is the slope of $y$ on $x$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the covariance by the variance of the predictor.

byKey.var-y: You divided by $\mathrm{Var}(y)$. That is the slope of $x$ on $y$.
byKey.upside: You put the variance over the covariance. The covariance goes on top.

explain.text: $b = \mathrm{Cov}(x, y)/\mathrm{Var}(x) = 1.8/1.5 = 1.2$. $\mathrm{Var}(y)$ is not needed for the slope of $y$ on $x$.

quiz.prose: For a stock on the market, $r = 0.5$, $s_x = 1$% and $s_y = 4$%, so the slope of $y$ on $x$ is $b = 2$.
quiz.question: What is the slope of $x$ on $y$?

options.why: You inverted $b$. The reverse regression has slope $r\,s_x/s_y = 0.5 \times 1/4$.
You assumed one line serves both ways. That holds only when $r = \pm 1$.
The correlation is the slope only when both spreads are equal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Swap the roles in $r\,s_y/s_x$.

explain.text: With $y$ as the predictor the slope is $r\,s_x/s_y = 0.5 \times 1/4 = 0.125$. Check: $b \times d = 2 \times 0.125 = 0.25 = r^2$. Inverting 2 gives 0.5, which is a different line.

quiz.question: What is the least squares slope?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Centre both variables at their means, 2 and 4, first.

byKey.raw: You used $\sum x_i y_i/\sum x_i^2 = 29/14$ without centring. That is the slope of a line forced through the origin.
byKey.upside: You divided $S_{xx}$ by $S_{xy}$. The products go on top.

explain.text: The means are 2 and 4, so the deviations are $(-1, 0, 1)$ and $(-2, -1, 3)$. The products add to $2 + 0 + 3 = 5$ and the squares to 2, so $b = 2.5$ and $a = 4 - 5 = -1$.
